# v0.2.1 — Critical: browser cache cleaning no longer exhausts system memory

## The problem

Cleaning a large browser cache (6 GB of data is real: Chrome/Edge/Brave
caches are hundreds of thousands of tiny `f_000123` files) could consume all
available RAM and peg the CPU at 100%, getting processes killed by the OS.
Three causes worked together:

1. **One finding per file.** The browser scan emitted a `Finding` for every
   cached file, so 6 GB became ~300,000 entries serialized to the frontend,
   held in the UI state and sent back over IPC for cleaning.
2. **Per-file recycle-bin operations.** Cleaning called the OS trash once
   per file. On Windows the Shell API creates recycle-bin metadata per item;
   with hundreds of thousands of items the Explorer and the app itself blow
   through RAM.
3. **No space reclaimed.** Moving 6 GB to the trash does not free a single
   byte until the trash is emptied — pointless for caches the browser
   rebuilds anyway.

## The fix

- **One finding per cache directory** (`Cache`, `Cache_Data`, `Code Cache`,
  `GPUCache`, `CacheStorage`, `cache2`, `startupCache`, …). Discovery never
  descends into a cache tree; the directory is the candidate, with the whole
  tree size summed into it. 6 GB of cache is now ~10–40 findings instead of
  hundreds of thousands.
- **In-place purge, not the trash.** Browser caches are regenerable, so
  cleaning removes the directory and recreates it empty (so the browser finds
  its cache root). Space is freed immediately. Everything else — duplicates,
  messenger media, large & old files — still goes to the trash and can be
  restored.
- **Purge safety guard.** The purge command only accepts paths that live
  inside a known browser root *and* carry a cache-like path component; it
  never follows symlinks. User-configured exclusions are honored in both
  directions: a cache inside an excluded folder is skipped, and so is a
  cache that *contains* an excluded folder.
- **Honest UI.** The browser card now warns that cache folders are deleted
  permanently (browsers rebuild them automatically), and mixed selections
  spell out what goes to the trash and what is deleted in place.
- **Walker thread cap (8).** Directory walking is syscall-bound and
  saturates well below the core counts of large machines; the cap keeps queue
  bursts proportional on 32-thread boxes.
- **RubyGems caches (`.gem`) are now excluded** from scans, alongside
  `.npm`, `.cargo` and friends.

**Upgrade note**: close your browsers before cleaning locked cache files;
any file the browser holds open shows up as a failure instead of taking the
system down.
